raw_case_text:
During the period of March 2009 till Febraury 2010, 75 PCNLs were performed in our unit. The standard technique followed for the procedure is explained in brief. Retrograde catheter (5fr.) was placed in the ipsilateral ureter under fluoroscopy in supine position. The patient was then placed in the prone position and the puncture was made using a three-part needle (Angiomed1.3 mm (17.5G)) under fluoroscopy control after retrograde opacification of the pelvicaliceal system via the ureteral catheter. An angle tip terumo wire (Radifocus; Terumo wire) was then positioned in the upper ureter. The tract was then dilated, initially using serial Teflon dilators up to 10fr. followed by placement of Alken's rod. The subsequent dilatation was achieved using serial Alken metal dilators and an Amplatz sheath (Cook Surgical) of adequate caliber used (Size 26/28/30 Fr.). The PCNL was then completed using Wolf nephroscope (24fr.) and pneumatic lithotripsy. An adequate-size nephrostomy was placed at the end of the procedure. All our patients recovered well. Nephrostomy was removed on the second postoperative day after the check X-ray KUB The nephrostomy tract site was then dressed with sterile dressing. Patient was discharged with instructions to remove the dressing after 72 h and follow up after one month if asymptomatic.
To keep the cost of the procedure reasonable we reuse the puncture needle, Teflon dilators, and the Amplatz sheath. All of these were rinsed adequately immediately after the end of the procedure and blow-dried. They were then placed along with the nephroscope in a 2% glutaraldehyde solution for a minimum of 45 min prior to the next procedure.
Six of our 75 patients presented with persistent discharge from the nephrostomy site. "Non-healing" was defined as nephrostomy sites that had not healed within three to four weeks after nephrostomy removal. [Table 1] gives the clinical details and mode of presentation of these patients. Average age of presentation was 39.2 + 12 years. Of the six patients four were males and two females. Four patients had undergone the procedure on the right side and the remaining two on the left side. None of the patients had a previous history suggestive of TB and had a normal chest X-ray. Average time of presentation was 35.5 + 6.8 days. The commonest symptom was mild pain and minimal but persistent discharge for the nephrostomy site.
On examination, initially it appeared like a simple wound infection with erythema [Figure 1a and b]. Patients were initially started on anti-staphylococcal medication (Linizolid 600 mg twice a day) with wound dressing. The wound did show signs of healing on subsequent dressings but then again erupted with discharge. The wounds were then explored under local anesthesia and the tissue excised was sent for histopathology. The histopathology of the tissue was suggestive of TB, with caseating granuloma that contained Langerhan's giant cells [Figure 2a and b].
Patients were then started on antitubercular medication:four drugs, (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for the first two months and then two drugs (rifampicin and isoniazid) for the remaining four months:in consultation with a dermatologist and this is in accordance with the current literature. Subsequently the wounds healed as the patients responded to the antitubercular medication. Average time to complete wound healing was 22 + 6 days after the start of antitubercular medication. All these patients have completed six months' follow-up and are doing fine.

subjective.chief_complaint: Six patients (mean age 39.2 ± 12 years; 4 males, 2 females) presenting with persistent discharge from nephrostomy tract sites following percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six out of 75 patients who underwent percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) presented at an average of 35.5 ± 6.8 days post-procedure with mild pain and persistent, non-healing discharge from their nephrostomy tract sites that failed to close 3 to 4 weeks after catheter removal. Four patients had right-sided and two had left-sided procedures. They were initially treated with oral linezolid (600 mg twice daily) and local wound dressings for suspected staphylococcal surgical site infection, demonstrating transient improvement followed by recurrent persistent discharge, leading to surgical wound exploration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for renal calculi using puncture needles, Teflon dilators, Amplatz sheaths, and nephroscopes reprocessed via 45-minute immersion in 2% glutaraldehyde. None of the patients had a prior history suggestive of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Mild local wound pain, persistent cutaneous discharge from nephrostomy site. Denies fever, weight loss, hematuria, or pulmonary symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Nephrostomy wound sites exhibited erythema and continuous minimal to moderate seropurulent discharge without systemic signs of sepsis.
objective.routine_investigations: Postoperative check plain radiographs of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) were satisfactory. Chest radiographs were normal in all six patients.
objective.advanced_workup: Local surgical wound exploration was performed under local anesthesia with complete excision of the non-healing sinus tracts and surrounding granulation tissue for histopathological examination.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Iatrogenic cutaneous tuberculosis of the nephrostomy tract secondary to contaminated reused surgical instruments (inadequate glutaraldehyde disinfection of PCNL equipment).
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological examination of excised nephrostomy tract tissue demonstrated characteristic caseating granulomas with Langhans multinucleated giant cells diagnostic of tuberculosis.
Management and outcome: Initial empiric anti-staphylococcal therapy with linezolid failed. Initiated on standard antitubercular therapy: 4-drug intensive phase (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for 2 months, followed by a 2-drug continuation phase (rifampicin and isoniazid) for 4 months. Complete wound healing was achieved at a mean of 22 ± 6 days following initiation of ATT. All six patients completed 6 months of follow-up without recurrence.
